name: Imperial Green
lede: Imperial green is a nineteenth-century name for a copper-arsenic green related to emerald green, and today's swatch is a clean mid green far brighter than the dull pigment the trade manuals describe.

sections.title: Two things with one name
sections.body:
The swatch is from the Maerz and Paul dictionary of 1930, plate 18, which records the name from 1853 [1]. It is a clear, fairly light green, nearest the name [[emerald]] (about 6 units of ΔE away) [1].

The pigment is a different matter. The British dictionary of colour words says simply to see emerald green [2], and the pigment reference lists imperial green among the names and variants of the copper-arsenic greens, with Paris green, Schweinfurt green, Vienna green and Brunswick green [3][2]. Those greens are the family of [[emerald-green]], [[scheele-s-green]] and [[brunswick-green]] [3].

sections.title: What the pigment was
sections.body:
Descriptions differ. A 1906 manual by Zerr and Rübencamp calls imperial green one of countless products of varying proportions of arsenic, copper sulphate and vinegar, and describes the dull kind as having no special covering power and sitting between emerald green and Neuwied lime green [3]. Mayer, writing in 1991, describes it as an emerald green carrying an inert filler [3].

Both accounts place it close to emerald green, one as a dull kind and the other as one carrying a filler, but neither gives a date for its invention, and the reference itself calls the use of these names within the group loose [3].

sections.title: In other greens' recipes
sections.body:
The name turns up as an ingredient in other trade names. Kirchberg green, according to Zerr and Rübencamp, was 40 to 50 parts imperial green mixed with 50 to 60 parts baryte [3]. Mitis green, by the same authors, was 35 to 55 parts emerald green and 45 to 65 parts imperial green, although another source uses Mitis green for other copper-arsenic compounds [3]. Neuwied green, which contains baryte and other fillers, is closely related to both Brunswick green and imperial green [3].

The family was toxic. The dictionary notes that Schweinfurt green, the group's best-known member, was used in wallpaper and was blamed in the 1860s for a number of deaths from arsenic fumes [2].

sections.title: The word imperial
sections.body:
The dictionary explains that *imperial* was first used for imperial yellow and then borrowed by other colors with pretensions of majesty [2]. Its entries include imperial blue, a deep blue dye, imperial red, a deep bluish red, and imperial yellow, a deep yellow taken from the porcelain reserved for the Chinese court [2]. Our own colors [[imperial-blue]] and [[imperial-red]] share the prefix.

A bibliography in Finlay's book on gems lists a work on imperial green jade, so the phrase is also used for a prized jade color [4]. The books we hold do not explain it, and it is a separate use from the pigment.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive, 2 of 23,781 paintings contain this green on at least five per cent of the canvas, within six units of ΔE [5]. They are Van Gogh's [[painting:nga-72328|Roses]] of 1890, where it covers 10 per cent, and Delaunay's [[painting:nga-52397|Political Drama]] of 1914, at 7.6 per cent [5]. The swatch has a contrast of only 2.4 to 1 against white [5].

These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and a color match is not a pigment test [5].
